Policy_Name: Increase in National Security Levy (NSL) to 15%
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Kumaratunga government raised the National Security Levy (NSL) from 5.5% to 6.5% and subsequently introduced broader emergency revenue surcharges to fund escalating civil war defense expenditure in the North-East.
Affected_Sectors: All Market; Manufacturing; Retail; Imports
Expected_Economic_Channel: Fiscal tightening; Corporate taxation; Inflationary expectations
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Annual Report 2000

Policy_Name: Presentation of the 2000 National Budget
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President and Minister of Finance Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga presented the 2000 national budget in Parliament. It rationalized import duty tariffs into two main bands (10% and 25%) while raising the National Security Levy (NSL) to fund expanding defense spending amidst escalating civil war costs.
Affected_Sectors: Macroeconomy, Import/Export Trade, Retail & Consumer Goods, Defense Sector
Expected_Economic_Channel: Higher NSL and import tariffs increased tax revenues but added cost-push inflationary pressures; defense spending crowded out capital development expenditure.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Central Bank of Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Enforcement of Nationwide War Footing Public Security Regulations
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Following the fall of the Elephant Pass military complex to the LTTE, President Kumaratunga invoked strict Public Security Act regulations placing the country on a total war footing, banning non-essential development projects and restricting press freedom.
Affected_Sectors: All Market; Construction; Tourism
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence; Sovereign-risk expectations; Foreign-investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Parliament of Sri Lanka Hansard

Policy_Name: Introduction of Emergency Defense Fiscal Package and Import Surcharges
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Following the loss of the strategic Elephant Pass military base to the LTTE, the government enacted an emergency fiscal package that increased the National Security Levy (NSL) from 6.5% to 7.5% and imposed a 10% surcharge on non-essential imports. The measures aimed to rapidly mobilize revenue to purchase emergency defense hardware.
Affected_Sectors: Import/Export, Manufacturing, Consumer Goods, Transport
Expected_Economic_Channel: Increased import surcharges and NSL squeezed corporate profit margins, raised consumer price inflation, and depressed import volumes.
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Annual Report 2000

Policy_Name: Floating of the Sri Lankan Rupee (LKR)
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka officially decided to float the Sri Lankan Rupee, abandoning the managed crawling peg exchange rate system amidst dwindling foreign reserves caused by war costs and oil price shocks.
Affected_Sectors: Banking; Finance; Imports; Exports; Manufacturing
Expected_Economic_Channel: Foreign exchange availability; Import cost; Export competitiveness; Inflationary expectations
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Press Release

Policy_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Floats the Sri Lankan Rupee (LKR)
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka abandoned the managed crawling-band exchange rate system and allowed the Sri Lankan Rupee to float freely against foreign currencies. The decision was taken to halt rapid depletion of foreign exchange reserves caused by high oil prices and heavy defense spending.
Affected_Sectors: Foreign Exchange Market, Banking, Import-Dependent Sectors, Export Sector, Fuel & Energy
Expected_Economic_Channel: Immediate LKR depreciation (~6.6% overnight) boosted export competitiveness (apparel, tea) but sharply increased import costs, fuel prices, and imported inflation.
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka / International Monetary Fund (IMF)

Policy_Name: Presentation of the 2001 National Budget
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Deputy Minister of Finance Prof. G.L. Peiris presented the 2001 national budget in Parliament. The budget featured a 40% surtax on import duties, an increase in NSL to 6.5%, price hikes on petroleum and utilities, and record military allocations of LKR 63.4 billion.
Affected_Sectors: Energy, Transport, Manufacturing, Imports, Consumer Goods
Expected_Economic_Channel: High indirect taxes and utility tariff hikes reduced household disposable income and squeezed private sector profitability while attempting to curb fiscal deficit.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Sri Lanka Ceasefire Agreement (CFA)
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe signed a Norwegian-brokered Permanent Ceasefire Agreement (CFA) with the LTTE, bringing an end to open hostilities and opening the way for peace negotiations and major economic revitalization.
Affected_Sectors: All Market; Tourism; Hotels; Construction; Banking; Plantations
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence; Foreign-investor confidence; Sovereign-risk expectations; Tourism expectations
Source_1_Name: Secretariat for Coordinating the Peace Process (SCOPP)

Policy_Name: Signing of Permanent Ceasefire Agreement (CFA) with LTTE
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe and LTTE leader Velupillai Prabhakaran signed a bilateral Permanent Ceasefire Agreement (CFA) mediated by the Norwegian Government. The truce formally suspended active military conflict, reopened major transport arteries (A9 highway), and established the Sri Lanka Monitoring Mission (SLMM).
Affected_Sectors: Tourism, Construction, Transport & Logistics, Agriculture, Banking & Financial Services, Real Estate
Expected_Economic_Channel: Elimination of active war risk sharply reduced defense spending, revitalized tourist arrivals, unlocked international donor assistance, and drove a multi-year bull run on the CSE.
Source_1_Name: United Nations Peacemaker / Secretariat for Coordinating the Peace Process (SCOPP)

Policy_Name: Value Added Tax (VAT) Act No. 14 of 2002
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Finance Minister KN Choksy presented the 2002 Budget introducing Value Added Tax (VAT) at two rates (10% and 20%) to replace the Goods and Services Tax (GST) and National Security Levy (NSL) effective August 1, 2002.
Affected_Sectors: All Market; Retail; Consumer Goods; Telecommunications; Manufacturing
Expected_Economic_Channel: Fiscal tightening; Corporate taxation; Consumer demand
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka Budget Speech 2002

Policy_Name: Presentation of the 2002 Reform-Oriented National Budget
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Minister of Finance K.N. Choksy presented the 2002 national budget in Parliament under the UNF administration. The budget focused on fiscal deficit reduction, cutting public expenditure, abolishing the National Security Levy (NSL), and announcing the introduction of Value Added Tax (VAT) to replace GST.
Affected_Sectors: Corporate Sector, Banking, Retail, Import/Export Trade
Expected_Economic_Channel: Tax simplification and removal of cascading turnover levies improved business confidence, stimulated investment, and targeted medium-term fiscal deficit contraction.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Central Bank of Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Enactment and Implementation of Value Added Tax (VAT) Act No. 14 of 2002
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The government formally replaced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) and the Goods Turnover Tax (BTT) with a dual-rate Value Added Tax (VAT) framework (10% standard rate for essential items, 20% for luxury goods).
Affected_Sectors: Retail Trade, Manufacturing, Wholesale, Import/Export, Services
Expected_Economic_Channel: Broadened the indirect tax base and streamlined compliance; initially caused minor price adjustments but improved fiscal revenue transparency.
Source_1_Name: Department of Inland Revenue / World Bank

Policy_Name: Opening of Sri Lanka Telecom (SLT) 12% State Equity IPO on CSE
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The government launched the privatization of a 12% stake in Sri Lanka Telecom (SLT) through an Initial Public Offering (IPO) on the Colombo Stock Exchange, offering 216 million ordinary shares to local and foreign investors to raise LKR 3.24 billion.
Affected_Sectors: Telecommunications, Capital Markets (CSE), Foreign Institutional Investment
Expected_Economic_Channel: Deepened capital market liquidity, attracted substantial foreign portfolio equity inflows, and established a benchmark for SOE privatization.
Source_1_Name: Sri Lanka Telecom Annual Report 2002 / Daily News

Policy_Name: Release of 'Regaining Sri Lanka: Vision and Strategy for Accelerated Development'
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe unveiled the comprehensive 'Regaining Sri Lanka' economic blueprint. The policy detailed structural reforms in labor laws, land ownership, deregulation of state monopolies, privatization, and target economic growth rates of 8–10%.
Affected_Sectors: Infrastructure, Manufacturing, Agriculture, Labor Market, Real Estate, Financial Services
Expected_Economic_Channel: Unlocked international concessionary aid ($4.5 billion pledged at Tokyo Donor Conference) and encouraged long-term private sector capital expenditure.
Source_1_Name: Government of Sri Lanka Policy Document / IMF

Policy_Name: Lanka IOC Entry and Privatization of Petroleum Distribution
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The government signed a formal agreement with Indian Oil Corporation (Lanka IOC), transferring 100 Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) retail stations and granting a 30-year lease for the Trincomalee oil tank farm. This ended CPC's long-standing state monopoly in petroleum retail.
Affected_Sectors: Energy, Fuel Retailing, Transportation, Storage & Logistics
Expected_Economic_Channel: Introduced market competition, upgraded retail fueling infrastructure, and reduced government fiscal burden from energy subsidies.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Energy / Lanka IOC PLC Annual Report

Policy_Name: Sale of 90% Equity in Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation (SLIC)
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Public Enterprises Reform Commission (PERC) finalized the sale of a 90% stake in state-owned Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation (SLIC) to the Distilleries-Spence Consortium (led by DCSL / Harry Jayawardena) for LKR 6.05 billion.
Affected_Sectors: Insurance, Financial Services, Capital Markets, Banking
Expected_Economic_Channel: Infused private sector capital into the insurance industry and generated substantial fiscal revenue for the Treasury.
Source_1_Name: PERC / Daily News / Supreme Court Case Archives

Policy_Name: 2003 Constitutional Crisis & Emergency Declaration
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Chandrika Kumaratunga prorogued Parliament, declared a state of emergency, and sacked three key Cabinet Ministers (Defence, Interior, and Mass Media) from the UNP government while PM Ranil Wickremesinghe was visiting Washington DC.
Affected_Sectors: All Market; Banking; Foreign Investment
Expected_Economic_Channel: Political uncertainty; Government stability; Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Official Gazette Extraordinary

Policy_Name: Presentation of 2004 National Budget Amidst Political Standoff
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Minister of Finance K.N. Choksy presented the 2004 national budget in Parliament during the ongoing executive-legislative crisis. The budget proposed further reduction of fiscal deficits to 6.8% of GDP, rationalization of civil service expenditure, and financial sector tax reforms.
Affected_Sectors: Banking, Financial Services, Public Sector Employment, Macroeconomy
Expected_Economic_Channel: Proposed expenditure constraints were overshadowed by political instability, limiting implementation certainty.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Central Bank of Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Presentation of the 2005 National Budget by Minister Sarath Amunugama
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Minister of Finance Sarath Amunugama presented the 2005 national budget under the UPFA administration. The budget introduced a dual VAT rate (9% and 18%), launched the Economic Service Charge (ESC), expanded public sector employment, and increased fertilizer subsidies for agriculture.
Affected_Sectors: Agriculture, Public Sector, Corporate Taxation, Retail & Wholesale Trade
Expected_Economic_Channel: Raised public sector wage bills and agricultural subsidies, increasing fiscal deficit pressures while giving short-term relief to rural farmers and state workers.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Central Bank of Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Government Enacts Post-Tsunami Tax Exemptions and Reconstruction Framework
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Following the catastrophic December 26, 2004 tsunami, the government announced tax and import duty exemptions on relief equipment, building materials, and emergency vehicles, while creating the Task Force for Rebuilding the Nation (TAFREN) to channel international aid.
Affected_Sectors: Construction, Building Materials, Real Estate, Banking, Import/Export Trade
Expected_Economic_Channel: Foreign aid inflows (~$3B pledged) and tax waivers boosted construction sector activity, offsetting immediate economic devastation along coastal regions.
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Annual Report 2005 / World Bank

Policy_Name: Signing of Post-Tsunami Operational Management Structure (P-TOMS)
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Sri Lankan government and LTTE signed the P-TOMS agreement to jointly manage $3 billion in international tsunami reconstruction funds in northern and eastern coastal zones. The move caused coalition partner JVP to pull out of the UPFA government on June 16, reducing UPFA to a minority.
Affected_Sectors: Construction, Infrastructure Aid Disbursement, Capital Markets
Expected_Economic_Channel: Facilitated donor aid disbursement mechanisms to North-East, but created political coalition instability in Colombo.
Source_1_Name: Daily News Sri Lanka / TamilNet / Encyclopedia.com

Policy_Name: Presentation of 2006 National Budget under 'Mahinda Chinthana' Policy
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Newly elected President and Finance Minister Mahinda Rajapaksa presented the 2006 national budget in Parliament. Built around the 'Mahinda Chinthana' manifesto, it expanded public sector infrastructure investment, doubled fertilizer subsidies, increased civil service salaries, and raised revenue through wealth taxes and levies.
Affected_Sectors: Agriculture, Construction & Public Infrastructure, Public Sector, Corporate Tax
Expected_Economic_Channel: Accelerated state-led infrastructure spending (ports, power plants, roads) and rural welfare, boosting GDP growth while expanding government borrowing and fiscal deficit.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Central Bank of Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Presentation of Sri Lanka Budget 2007
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President and Minister of Finance Mahinda Rajapaksa presented the 2007 Budget in Parliament under the policy framework of 'Mahinda Chinthana'. The budget increased defence spending significantly to Rs. 139 billion due to renewed hostilities with the LTTE while granting tax relief to domestic agricultural producers and small businesses. Fiscal deficit target was set at 9.2% of GDP.
Affected_Sectors: Defence; Agriculture; Infrastructure; Public Finance
Expected_Economic_Channel: Higher fiscal deficit and defence expenditure increased inflationary pressures and government borrowing requirements.
Source_1_Name: Daily News Sri Lanka / Ministry of Finance

Policy_Name: Gazetting of Prevention and Prohibition of Terrorism Emergency Regulations
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Mahinda Rajapaksa issued Gazette Extraordinary No. 1474/5 enacting stringent Emergency Regulations for the Prevention and Prohibition of Terrorism. The regulations banned organizations aiding terrorism, granted security forces wide powers of arrest and detention without warrant, and imposed restrictions on transport and logistics in high-security zones. The move formalized the resumption of full-scale conflict with the LTTE.
Affected_Sectors: Logistics; Shipping; Tourism; Insurance; Foreign Direct Investment
Expected_Economic_Channel: Elevated war risk premiums, increased security compliance costs for businesses, and dampening of foreign tourist arrivals.
Source_1_Name: Government Gazette of Sri Lanka / Daily News

Policy_Name: Central Bank Raises Policy Interest Rates by 50 Bps to Control Inflation
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) tightened monetary policy by hiking the Repurchase Rate by 50 bps to 10.50% and the Reverse Repurchase Rate to 12.00%. CBSL also restricted commercial banks' access to the reverse repo facility to drain excess liquidity. The action was aimed at arresting runaway inflation, which exceeded 19% annually due to war spending and high international oil prices.
Affected_Sectors: Banking; Real Estate; Consumer Credit; Capital Markets
Expected_Economic_Channel: Higher cost of credit constrained private sector borrowing and capital investment, while helping to anchor inflation expectations.
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Press Release

Policy_Name: Dismissal of Foreign Minister Mangala Samaraweera and Cabinet Colleagues
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Mahinda Rajapaksa dismissed Foreign Minister Mangala Samaraweera, Enterprise Development Minister Anura Bandaranaike, and Deputy Minister Sripathi Sooriyaarachchi from the Cabinet. The sackings followed growing internal dissent regarding human rights abuses, extrajudicial abductions, and coalition management. Samaraweera subsequently formed the SLFP (Mahajana Wing) opposition group.
Affected_Sectors: Governance; Foreign Relations; Trade Policy
Expected_Economic_Channel: Strained diplomatic relations with Western trade partners and EU authorities, threatening trade concessions such as GSP+.
Source_1_Name: TamilNet / Reuters / Daily News

Policy_Name: Presentation of Sri Lanka Budget 2008
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Mahinda Rajapaksa presented Budget 2008 in Parliament, boosting defence allocation to a record Rs. 166 billion to fund military offensives in the North and East. The budget introduced duty increases on luxury imports, enhanced excise taxes, and designated capital funding for major infrastructure projects including Hambantota Port and Norochcholai Power Plant.
Affected_Sectors: Defence; Import Trade; Power & Energy; Infrastructure
Expected_Economic_Channel: Fiscal expansion supported state-led infrastructure investment but sustained elevated government debt and double-digit inflation.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Daily News

Policy_Name: Presentation of Sri Lanka Budget 2009
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Mahinda Rajapaksa presented Budget 2009 amidst the onset of the Global Financial Crisis and intense final war operations. Defence allocation was raised to Rs. 177 billion. To offset declining tax revenue and global export shocks, the government introduced the Nation Building Tax (NBT) and increased tariff surcharges on imported non-essential goods.
Affected_Sectors: Manufacturing; Imports; Taxation; Defence
Expected_Economic_Channel: New turnover taxes and tariff protection broadened government revenue base but raised operational costs for domestic businesses.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Daily News

Policy_Name: Central Bank Takes Over Management of Seylan Bank PLC
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) invoked powers under the Monetary Law Act to dissolve the Board of Directors of Seylan Bank PLC following a deposit run triggered by the financial collapse of the un-regulated Golden Key Credit Card Company (a Ceylinco affiliate). CBSL appointed state-owned Bank of Ceylon to take over management and recapitalize Seylan Bank, averting a wider systemic banking crisis.
Affected_Sectors: Banking; Financial Services; Capital Markets
Expected_Economic_Channel: Decisive central bank intervention contained financial contagion, restored public depositor confidence, and protected financial stability.
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka / The Island

Policy_Name: Implementation of Nation Building Tax (NBT) Act No. 9 of 2009
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Sri Lankan government implemented the Nation Building Tax (NBT) at a rate of 1%-2% levied on the turnover of importers, manufacturers, and service providers. Revenue raised was dedicated to infrastructure development and national security financing. The tax expanded the indirect tax burden across commercial sectors.
Affected_Sectors: Wholesale & Retail; Manufacturing; Services; Imports
Expected_Economic_Channel: Increased transaction costs across business value chains, slightly dampening commercial profit margins while improving fiscal revenue.
Source_1_Name: Inland Revenue Department Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: IMF Approves $2.6 Billion Stand-By Arrangement for Sri Lanka
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Executive Board of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) approved a 20-month Stand-By Arrangement (SBA) of US$ 2.6 billion (SDR 1.65 billion) for Sri Lanka. The program aimed to rebuild foreign exchange reserves depleted during the final stages of the civil war, reduce fiscal deficits, and support post-war economic reconstruction.
Affected_Sectors: Macroeconomy; Foreign Exchange Market; Banking; Sovereign Debt
Expected_Economic_Channel: Restored gross official reserves, boosted international investor confidence, stabilized the Sri Lankan Rupee, and catalyzed capital market inflows.
Source_1_Name: International Monetary Fund (Press Release No. 09/266)

Policy_Name: Central Bank Cuts Policy Interest Rates to Stimulate Post-War Growth
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka reduced its Repurchase Rate and Reverse Repurchase Rate by 50 bps to 8.00% and 10.00% respectively. This continued a series of rate cuts initiated in early 2009 aimed at easing credit constraints, encouraging private sector borrowing, and supporting post-war economic recovery.
Affected_Sectors: Banking; Construction; Manufacturing; Capital Markets
Expected_Economic_Channel: Lower borrowing costs catalyzed private sector credit growth, commercial investment, and a bull run on the Colombo Stock Exchange.
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Press Release

Policy_Name: President Dissolves 13th Parliament of Sri Lanka
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Mahinda Rajapaksa dissolved Parliament two months prior to its term expiration and scheduled fresh parliamentary elections for April 8, 2010. The dissolution aimed to leverage presidential election momentum to secure a legislative supermajority for constitutional reforms.
Affected_Sectors: Governance; Legislative Approvals; Public Finance
Expected_Economic_Channel: Suspension of parliamentary legislative business until election of a new parliament.
Source_1_Name: Government Gazette Extraordinary / Parliament of Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Presentation of Post-War Budget 2010
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Mahinda Rajapaksa presented the delayed 2010 Budget to Parliament. The budget targeted a reduction in fiscal deficit to 8.0% of GDP, reduced import duties on machinery and raw materials to spur industrial investment, and expanded public sector capital expenditure on port, road, and power infrastructure.
Affected_Sectors: Construction; Capital Goods; Manufacturing; Infrastructure
Expected_Economic_Channel: Tariff relief on capital imports lowered industrial establishment costs, accelerating post-war GDP growth.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Daily News

Policy_Name: Central Bank Relaxes Foreign Exchange Controls and Treasury Bond Limits
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka announced comprehensive exchange control relaxations, permitting foreign investors to purchase up to 10% of total outstanding Treasury Bonds, liberalizing foreign currency accounts, and removing restrictions on outward remittances for corporate investments. The policy aimed to attract foreign capital inflows and reduce public debt interest costs.
Affected_Sectors: Banking; Capital Markets; Treasury Securities; Foreign Direct Investment
Expected_Economic_Channel: Inflow of foreign portfolio capital into sovereign debt, lowering government borrowing yields and improving rupee liquidity.
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Press Release

Policy_Name: Parliament Passes 18th Amendment Abolishing Presidential Term Limits
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Parliament passed the 18th Amendment to the Constitution by 161 votes to 17. The amendment abolished the two-term limit for the Executive Presidency and replaced the independent Constitutional Council with a Presidential-appointed Parliamentary Council, centralizing executive authority over independent state commissions.
Affected_Sectors: Governance; Legal Framework; Sovereign Risk
Expected_Economic_Channel: Enhanced medium-term policy continuity under executive stability, balanced against long-term governance risks from weakened institutional checks and balances.
Source_1_Name: Parliament of Sri Lanka / Transparency International Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Presentation of Post-War Budget 2011 with Structural Tax Reforms
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Mahinda Rajapaksa presented Budget 2011 to Parliament, introducing major tax simplification. Maximum corporate and personal income tax rates were reduced from 35% to 28%, financial sector VAT was simplified, and import tariffs were restructured. The budget targeted 8%+ GDP growth and a fiscal deficit target of 6.8% of GDP.
Affected_Sectors: Corporate Sector; Financial Services; Construction; Manufacturing
Expected_Economic_Channel: Substantial reductions in corporate tax rates and simplified tax compliance stimulated private domestic and foreign direct investment.
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / FT.lk / Daily News

Policy_Name: 2012 Budget Speech & 3% Devaluation Announcement
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Mahinda Rajapaksa presented the 2012 Budget in Parliament, proposing total expenditure of LKR 1.22 Trillion while announcing an immediate 3% official devaluation of the LKR against USD to support export trade balance.
Affected_Sectors: Banking; Imports; Exports; Automobiles
Expected_Economic_Channel: Import cost; Inflationary expectations; Export competitiveness
Source_1_Name: Parliament of Sri Lanka Hansard

Policy_Name: CBSL Flexible Exchange Rate Policy & Interest Rate Hike
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka announced a major policy shift allowing greater exchange rate flexibility, resulting in an immediate 9% LKR devaluation, while hiking key policy interest rates by 50 bps to curb credit growth.
Affected_Sectors: Banking; Finance; Imports; Exports; Manufacturing
Expected_Economic_Channel: Interest-rate expectations; Foreign exchange availability; Import cost
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Press Release

Policy_Name: Parliamentary Resolution Impeaching Chief Justice Shirani Bandaranayake
Policy_Subcategory: Impeachment of Chief Justice & Constitutional Crisis
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Parliament voted 155 to 49 to pass an impeachment resolution against Chief Justice Shirani Bandaranayake following a contentious Select Committee inquiry, despite Supreme Court rulings declaring the procedure unconstitutional.
Affected_Sectors: All Market; Foreign Investment; Governance
Expected_Economic_Channel: Rule of law; Foreign-investor confidence; Governance risk
Source_1_Name: Parliament of Sri Lanka Hansard

Policy_Name: PUCSL 35-50% Electricity Tariff Revision
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Public Utilities Commission enforced a major electricity tariff hike averaging 35% to 50% across residential, industrial, and commercial categories to curb Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) operational losses.
Affected_Sectors: Manufacturing; Hotels; Retail; Energy; Consumer Goods
Expected_Economic_Channel: Corporate cost structure; Inflationary expectations; Industrial margins
Source_1_Name: PUCSL Official Tariff Announcement

Policy_Name: 2015 Interim Budget & One-off Super Gains Tax
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Finance Minister Ravi Karunanayake presented the 100-day interim budget, introducing a retrospective 25% Super Gains Tax on companies earning over LKR 2 Billion profit in FY2013/14, sparking sharp market reaction.
Affected_Sectors: All Market; Large Cap Corporates; Telecom; Banking; Beverage & Tobacco
Expected_Economic_Channel: Corporate taxation; Investor confidence; Retrospective regulatory uncertainty
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Budget Speech 2015

Policy_Name: IMF Executive Board Approves US$1.5 Billion Extended Fund Facility for Sri Lanka
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Executive Board of the International Monetary Fund approved a 36-month Extended Fund Facility (EFF) arrangement for Sri Lanka amounting to approximately SDR 1.1 billion (US$1.5 billion). The program aimed to support economic stability, rebuild international reserves, and institute fiscal consolidation.
Affected_Sectors: Financials; Government Securities; All Sectors
Expected_Economic_Channel: Restored international investor confidence, provided critical balance of payments support, and anchored medium-term fiscal deficit reduction targets under structural IMF benchmarks.
Source_1_Name: IMF Press Release

Policy_Name: Sri Lanka Parliament Passes Value Added Tax (VAT) Increase to 15%
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Parliament of Sri Lanka approved the Value Added Tax (VAT) Amendment Bill, raising the standard VAT rate from 11% to 15% and expanding the tax base to include healthcare and telecommunications services, effective November 1, 2016. This followed a court suspension of an earlier May 2016 attempt due to procedural flaws.
Affected_Sectors: Consumer Goods; Telecommunications; Healthcare; Retail
Expected_Economic_Channel: Boosted government revenue collection to support fiscal deficit targets under the IMF program, but caused temporary inflationary pressure and dampened short-term consumer retail demand.
Source_1_Name: EconomyNext

Policy_Name: Finance Minister Presents Sri Lanka 2017 National Budget
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Finance Minister Ravi Karunanayake presented the 2017 Budget targeting a reduction of the budget deficit to 4.6% of GDP. The budget prioritized fiscal consolidation, shifting the tax structure toward direct taxation, simplifying corporate tax slabs, and introducing capital gains tax.
Affected_Sectors: Financials; Capital Markets; Automotive; Consumer Goods
Expected_Economic_Channel: Signaled strong commitment to fiscal discipline and revenue expansion under IMF supervision, lowering sovereign credit risk while adding tax obligations for corporate profits.
Source_1_Name: Reuters

Policy_Name: Sri Lanka Signs $1.12 Billion Agreement Leasing Hambantota Port to China Merchants Port
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) signed a 99-year concession agreement with China Merchants Port Holdings (CMPort) for the management and operation of the Hambantota Port for $1.12 billion. The port was formally handed over to the joint venture on December 9, 2017.
Affected_Sectors: Ports & Shipping; Logistics; Government Securities; Financials
Expected_Economic_Channel: Provided substantial foreign exchange inflows of $1.12 billion to bolster central bank reserves and pay off high-cost foreign debt, though sparking geopolitical debate over debt sustainability.
Source_1_Name: The Hindu

Policy_Name: Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera Presents 2018 'Enterprise Sri Lanka' Budget
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera presented the 2018 National Budget themed 'Enterprise Sri Lanka', focusing on private sector entrepreneurship, green economy initiatives, trade liberalization, and targeting a fiscal deficit of 4.8% of GDP.
Affected_Sectors: SMEs; Automotive; Exports; Financials; Green Energy
Expected_Economic_Channel: Stimulated SME investments, green energy, and export competitiveness while pursuing revenue-based fiscal consolidation to lower public debt levels.
Source_1_Name: EconomyNext

Policy_Name: Sri Lanka's New Inland Revenue Act 2017 Comes Into Force
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The new Inland Revenue Act No. 24 of 2017 officially took effect on April 1, 2018, establishing a modernized direct tax framework, widening the tax net, rationalizing tax incentives, and introducing expanded withholding taxes on investment returns.
Affected_Sectors: Financials; Corporates; High-Net-Worth Individuals; All Sectors
Expected_Economic_Channel: Improved direct tax architecture and government revenue stability, reducing structural dependence on regressive indirect taxes.
Source_1_Name: Daily FT

Policy_Name: President Sirisena Dismisses PM Ranil Wickremesinghe and Appoints Mahinda Rajapaksa
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Maithripala Sirisena abruptly sacked Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe and appointed opposition leader Mahinda Rajapaksa as Prime Minister, initiating a 52-day constitutional crisis. Wickremesinghe denounced the move as unconstitutional and refused to vacate office, maintaining he commanded a parliamentary majority.
Affected_Sectors: All Sectors; Government Securities; Financials; Tourism
Expected_Economic_Channel: Triggered sovereign credit rating downgrades (Moody's, S&P, Fitch), capital outflows, currency depreciation, suspension of foreign aid agreements, and intense market uncertainty.
Source_1_Name: Reuters

Policy_Name: Sri Lanka Supreme Court Rules Parliament Dissolution Unconstitutional; Wickremesinghe Reinstated
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: A seven-judge bench of the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that President Sirisena's dissolution of Parliament was illegal and unconstitutional. Mahinda Rajapaksa resigned on December 15, and Ranil Wickremesinghe was re-sworn as Prime Minister on December 16, ending the constitutional crisis.
Affected_Sectors: All Sectors; Financials; Government Securities
Expected_Economic_Channel: Re-established legal and constitutional order, stabilizing foreign exchange and bond markets and mitigating further credit rating downgrades.
Source_1_Name: Reuters

Policy_Name: Finance Minister Presents Delayed 2019 National Budget
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera presented the 2019 Budget titled 'Empowering People and Nurturing the Poor', four months delayed due to the 2018 constitutional crisis. The budget targeted a fiscal deficit of 4.4% of GDP and introduced tax relief for export, tourism, and housing sectors.
Affected_Sectors: Tourism; Exports; Housing; Financials
Expected_Economic_Channel: Restored formal fiscal policy continuity after months of interim vote-on-account spending, enabling the resumption of delayed IMF program disbursements.
Source_1_Name: EconomyNext

Policy_Name: Sri Lanka Cabinet Approves Sweeping Stimulus Tax Cuts
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The newly formed Cabinet under President Gotabaya Rajapaksa approved sweeping tax cuts, reducing VAT from 15% to 8%, abolishing the 2% Nation Building Tax (NBT), Economic Service Charge (ESC), and PAYE tax, while slashing corporate income taxes for key sectors, effective December 1, 2019.
Affected_Sectors: Consumer Goods; Retail; Construction; Financials; Government Securities
Expected_Economic_Channel: Provided immediate domestic demand stimulus and profit margin relief for businesses, but severely eroded government fiscal revenue (losing over 25% of tax receipts), triggering sovereign credit rating downgrades and elevated default risks.
Source_1_Name: Reuters

Policy_Name: Government Enacts Extraordinary Import Restrictions to Conserve Foreign Exchange
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Ministry of Finance issued Extraordinary Gazette No. 2171/5 under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, temporarily suspending imports of motor vehicles, non-essential consumer goods, electronics, and agricultural products to mitigate foreign reserve depletion during the pandemic.
Affected_Sectors: Automotive; Import/Trading; Retail; Consumer Electronics; Manufacturing
Expected_Economic_Channel: Conserved foreign currency reserves in the short term for sovereign debt service, but caused domestic supply bottlenecks, import price inflation, and business disruption for import-dependent sectors.
Source_1_Name: EconomyNext

Policy_Name: Sri Lanka Parliament Passes 20th Amendment Restoring Executive Powers
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Parliament passed the 20th Amendment to the Constitution with a 156-65 supermajority, certified by the Speaker on October 29. The amendment repealed key institutional checks of the 19th Amendment, concentrating broad executive powers in the President over appointments to the judiciary, election commission, and audit bodies.
Affected_Sectors: All Sectors; Governance / Public Policy
Expected_Economic_Channel: Centralized executive policymaking authority, streamlining policy execution but raising international concerns over institutional checks and balances and rule of law.
Source_1_Name: Reuters

Policy_Name: Prime Minister Mahinda Rajapaksa Presents 2021 Import-Substitution Budget
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Prime Minister and Finance Minister Mahinda Rajapaksa presented the 2021 National Budget targeting a fiscal deficit of 8.9% of GDP. The budget emphasized an import-substitution economic model, domestic manufacturing, agricultural production incentives, and guaranteed tax stability for 5 years.
Affected_Sectors: Agriculture; Manufacturing; Financials; Government Securities
Expected_Economic_Channel: Offered domestic production incentives but increased market concern over high debt-servicing burdens and wide fiscal deficits amidst shrinking foreign reserves.
Source_1_Name: EconomyNext

Policy_Name: Sri Lanka Enforces Complete Ban on Chemical Fertilizer and Agrochemical Imports
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Gotabaya Rajapaksa's administration issued Extraordinary Gazette No. 2226/48 on May 6, 2021 (following an April 27 Cabinet decision), banning the import of synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, and fungicides to enforce a 100% organic farming policy. The abrupt ban severely disrupted tea, rubber, and paddy cultivation, causing rice production to drop by over 30% and leading to food inflation and heavy reliance on imports before being partially rolled back in late 2021.
Affected_Sectors: Agriculture Sector (Paddy & Plantation Crops), Food & Beverage, Inflation & Trade Balance; Expected economic channel: Severe supply-side agricultural output shock driving up food inflation, reducing tea export earnings, and depleting foreign exchange reserves.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service / Sri Lanka Gazette No. 2226/48

Policy_Name: Central Bank Imposes 100% Cash Margin on Non-Essential Imports & Enforces De-Facto FX Peg
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: On September 8, 2021, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) imposed a mandatory 100% cash margin deposit requirement on letters of credit for over 600 non-essential consumer goods to preserve declining foreign reserves. Concurrently, CBSL maintained a rigid de-facto exchange rate ceiling of 200-203 LKR/USD through moral suasion and surrender rules, resulting in parallel market premiums and severe import shortages.
Affected_Sectors: Commercial Banking, Foreign Trade, Wholesale & Retail; Expected economic channel: Trade contraction, disincentivizing formal FX inflows, creating parallel market exchange rates, and causing shortages of imported input goods.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka Press Release / IMF

Policy_Name: Finance Minister Basil Rajapaksa Presents 2022 Budget Targeting 8.8% Fiscal Deficit
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Finance Minister Basil Rajapaksa presented the 2022 Budget to Parliament on November 12, 2021, targeting a budget deficit of 8.8% of GDP. The budget introduced a one-off 25% Surcharge Tax on high-earning firms (profits above Rs. 2 billion) and a Social Security Contribution Levy, while opting against structural tax reforms required to restore external debt sustainability.
Affected_Sectors: Corporate Sector, Public Finance, Taxation, Banking; Expected economic channel: One-off profit tax burden on corporate earnings and lack of structural fiscal adjustment, failing to avert sovereign rating downgrades.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Ada Derana

Policy_Name: Central Bank Abandons LKR Peg and Permits Exchange Rate Flexibility
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: On March 7, 2022, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka announced it would allow 'greater flexibility' in the exchange rate, setting an initial soft cap of 230 LKR/USD. Rapid reserve exhaustion forced a full currency float, resulting in the LKR depreciating over 70% to exceed 360 LKR/USD by April 2022 and triggering hyperinflation across fuel, power, food, and medicines.
Affected_Sectors: Macroeconomy, Energy Sector, Manufacturing, Consumer Goods; Expected economic channel: Immediate imported inflation shock and cost-of-living crisis, offset by eventual normalization of official worker remittance channels.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka / Al Jazeera

Policy_Name: Ministry of Finance Formally Suspends External Debt Servicing (Pre-Emptive Default)
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: On April 12, 2022, the Ministry of Finance officially declared an interim suspension of debt service payments on all external public debt (~$51 billion), including International Sovereign Bonds and bilateral loans. Officials stated this emergency measure was necessary to preserve remaining foreign exchange for essential imports of fuel, food, and medicine while negotiating an IMF bailout.
Affected_Sectors: Sovereign Credit Markets, Banking System, Foreign Trade Finance; Expected economic channel: Immediate credit rating downgrade to Selective/Restricted Default, loss of international capital market access, and trade credit line freeze.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka Official Statement

Policy_Name: Prime Minister Mahinda Rajapaksa Resigns Following Violent Clashes in Colombo
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Prime Minister Mahinda Rajapaksa resigned on May 9, 2022, after government supporters attacked peaceful anti-government demonstrators at Temple Trees and Galle Face Green. The violence triggered nationwide anti-government riots, destruction of politicians' properties, and the collapse of the cabinet, forcing Mahinda Rajapaksa to evacuate to a naval base.
Affected_Sectors: Public Governance, National Security, Tourism & Business Operations; Expected economic channel: Severe political instability, disruption to government functions, and temporary freeze in IMF negotiations.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Al Jazeera / ConstitutionNet / Reuters

Policy_Name: President Gotabaya Rajapaksa Flees Country and Tenders Resignation via Email
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: Following mass public storming of the President's Secretariat on July 9, 2022, President Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled Sri Lanka to Singapore and submitted his official resignation letter via email to the Speaker of Parliament on July 14, 2022. Speaker Mahinda Yapa Abeywardena officially accepted and verified the resignation on July 15, ending the Gotabaya administration.
Affected_Sectors: Executive Branch, Sovereign Risk Perception, International Relations; Expected economic channel: Resolution of executive deadlock, paving the way for political stabilization and resumption of debt restructuring talks.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Al Jazeera / BBC News

Policy_Name: Parliament Elects Ranil Wickremesinghe as Executive President of Sri Lanka
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: In a secret parliamentary ballot on July 20, 2022, Ranil Wickremesinghe was elected as Sri Lanka's 8th Executive President, receiving 134 votes out of 225. He was sworn into office on July 21, 2022, establishing a government focused on fiscal stabilization, law enforcement, and IMF bailout execution.
Affected_Sectors: Government Administration, Financial Markets, Sovereign Debt Negotiations; Expected economic channel: Policy continuity, accelerated engagement with multilateral creditors, and stabilization of domestic essential supply lines.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Parliament of Sri Lanka / Al Jazeera

Policy_Name: President Wickremesinghe Presents Interim Budget 2022 Raising VAT to 15%
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President and Finance Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe presented the 2022 Interim Budget to Parliament on August 30, 2022, to align fiscal targets with IMF staff-level recommendations. Main policy actions included raising VAT from 12% to 15% effective September 1, 2022, and bolstering funding for social safety net programs.
Affected_Sectors: Retail Trade, Consumer Prices, State Revenues; Expected economic channel: Increases indirect tax receipts and satisfies initial IMF precondition targets.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Daily FT

Policy_Name: President Wickremesinghe Presents 2023 Budget Aligned with IMF EFF Framework
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Ranil Wickremesinghe presented the 2023 Budget to Parliament on November 14, 2022, aiming for a primary surplus by 2025. The budget incorporated personal income tax hikes (up to 36%), corporate tax increases to 30%, utility tariff rationalization, and state-owned enterprise (SOE) restructuring plans.
Affected_Sectors: Corporate Sector, Public Sector Employment, High-Income Households; Expected economic channel: Fiscal consolidation via direct tax revenue growth and structural deficit reduction.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Ada Derana

Policy_Name: IMF Executive Board Approves $3 Billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) for Sri Lanka
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: On March 20, 2023, the IMF Executive Board approved a 48-month EFF arrangement of SDR 2.286 billion (~$3 billion) for Sri Lanka, unlocking an initial tranche of $333 million. The program set structural benchmarks for fiscal consolidation, inflation targeting, financial stability, and anti-corruption reforms, enabling catalytic funding from World Bank and ADB.
Affected_Sectors: Sovereign Finance, External Sector, Banking System, Foreign Exchange; Expected economic channel: Rebuilding foreign exchange reserves, reducing sovereign risk premiums, and establishing exchange rate stability.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: IMF Press Release / Central Bank of Sri Lanka

Policy_Name: Parliament Approves Domestic Debt Optimization (DDO) Strategy
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Parliament of Sri Lanka passed the Domestic Debt Optimization (DDO) resolution on July 1, 2023 (122 votes to 62), following Cabinet approval on June 28. The strategy restructured domestic Treasury bonds held by superannuation funds (EPF/ETF) while preserving commercial bank solvency, satisfying a core requirement for foreign debt restructuring under the IMF program.
Affected_Sectors: Superannuation Funds, Banking System, Domestic Capital Markets; Expected economic channel: Reduced sovereign debt service burdens and lower interest rate environment at the expense of lower future pension yields.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Ada Derana

Policy_Name: President Wickremesinghe Presents 2024 Budget Focusing on Revenue Mobilization
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President Ranil Wickremesinghe presented the 2024 Budget to Parliament on November 13, 2023, targeting LKR 4.1 trillion in tax revenues. Key policy proposals included a Rs. 10,000 public sector cost-of-living allowance increase alongside planned VAT rate increases and exemption removals to meet IMF revenue targets.
Affected_Sectors: Public Employment, Fiscal Policy, Consumer Goods; Expected economic channel: Acceleration of revenue mobilization alongside cost-of-living adjustments for civil servants.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Ministry of Finance Sri Lanka / Lanka Puvath

Policy_Name: Value Added Tax (VAT) Increases to 18% and Removes 95 Tax Exemptions
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2023 took effect on January 1, 2024, raising the standard VAT rate from 15% to 18% and eliminating tax exemptions on 95 items (including fuel, domestic gas, and electricity). The measure aimed to elevate state tax revenues toward 12% of GDP under IMF program guidelines.
Affected_Sectors: Retail Trade, Energy & Utilities, Consumer Goods; Expected economic channel: One-off inflation spike (+2.5% to +3.0%) compressing real household incomes while significantly expanding government fiscal revenue.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Inland Revenue Department / HKTDC

Policy_Name: President Anura Kumara Dissanayake Presents First NPP Government Budget for 2025
Implementing_Authority: Cabinet of Ministers / Ministry of Finance
Policy_Summary: President and Minister of Finance Anura Kumara Dissanayake presented the 2025 Budget to Parliament on February 17, 2025. The budget targeted targeted relief for low-income families, income tax threshold adjustments, and expanded health and education capital outlays while preserving primary surplus commitments under the IMF EFF program.
Affected_Sectors: Social Welfare, Education & Health, Income Taxpayers, Infrastructure; Expected economic channel: Targeted social expenditure boosting domestic demand while preserving fiscal targets required by multilateral creditors.
Expected_Economic_Channel: Investor confidence
Source_1_Name: Parliament of Sri Lanka / Ministry of Finance
